issues.

Steve Buckland

---------- Forwarded message ----------
Date: Wed, 18 Oct 2006 08:34:16 +0100 (BST)
From: Steve Buckland <st...@mcs.st-andrews.ac.uk>
To: Robert McFarlane <rw...@swbell.net>
Subject: Re: [DIST-SAMP] Fwd: Re: Fwd: [DIST-SAMP] 3 sampling questions


> > In regards to question 1, sampling birds in a marine environment, I cannot
> > use a laser rangefinder to determine the distance from observer to bird, as
> > water absorbs the laser. A radar works very well to determine the distance.
> > So, theoretically, if the radar is mounted on a mobile boat, I can do either
> > line transects, or point transects if the boat is moved to various positions.
> > But there is no way to use Distance from a single, stationary observation
> > point. On land, the resources (habitat, food sources) are stationary and the
> > birds move between them. Over water, the resources are mobile. For example,
> > schools of fishes, the prey, are constantly moving. Birds, as predators of
> > the fish, may be more or less randomly distributed as they search for fish,
> > and watch other birds, but as soon as a school is detected the birds
> > aggregate. In addition, the water mass itself is constantly moving. If I
> > observe birds at some time interval, it is unlikely that I am observing the
> > same
> > birds. If I throw a bucket over to sample the water, I am not sampling the
> > same water. So, while the observation point is static, the environment is
> > dynamic. What is a reasonable time interval to consider the samples
> > independent?

The fact that the system is dynamic doesn't mean you can assume independence -
whatever the time interval. Your one point has some properties that remain
static, or relatively so - e.g. depth, water currents, proximity to some fixed
feature that the birds use, upwellings, or whatever. It cannot be regarded as
being representative of a wider area.

> > In regards to question 2, sampling a vertical plane, I know that the birds
> > will not be uniformly distributed. Most of them will be at lower heights
> > above the water. I see why that will not work.
> >
> > For question 3, the 22 degrees is the vertical angle, so 22/360 will not
> > work. The probability of detecting a bird increases with distance, out to a
> > certain point where the reflected signal is too weak to be detected, because
> > the area covered by the beam increases in both height and breadth. It is this
> > inability to detect a bird close to the observer that bothers me. It is
> > assumed that all birds at zero distance are detected, when, in fact, none
> > are.

I suggest you read up on point transect sampling. Also on 3D distance sampling
- see chapter 11 of the advanced distance sampling. The 22/360 factor is
relevant - it is simple trigonometry. The only complication arising from it
being a vertical angle is the one mentioned above - the vertical distribution
of birds is not uniform. Note that the area at distance zero for a point
transect sample is also zero - there will be no birds at the point. That
doesn't prevent us making the assumption that any bird there - if there were
one - would be certain to be detected.
Mathematically, you're taking limits as the distance tends to zero.

> > I am trying to design a study for a proposed offshore wind farm. Initially,
> > there will be one meteorological tower where I can mount a radar. Eventually
> > there may be two towers. Pending estimates of bird-rotor collision mortality
> > the area may be populated with wind turbines. But if Distance cannot be used
> > to estimate bird density from just one or two sampling points, there would
> > appear to be little reason to install radars on the towers. Do you have any
> > thoughts on this sampling problem?

It can tell you something about what might happen specifically at those
locations. Whether those locations reflect what might happen at other
locations then comes down to ecology, and understanding of the behavior of your
bird populations ... you can't rely on statistics to provide extrapolation from
just one or two sample locations.

Steve
